drills.q: What are the three steps of the backtracking template used to generate subsets, permutations, and combinations, and in what order do they always occur?
drills.a: Choose (add the element to the path or mark it used), explore (recurse one level deeper), un-choose (remove it from the path or unmark it used) -- un-choose always happens after the recursive call returns, before trying the next sibling.

drills.q: Why is the total time complexity of subset generation O(2^n * n) and not just O(2^n)?
drills.a: There are 2^n leaves in the recursion tree (one per subset), but each subset must actually be copied/built as an output, and a subset can have up to n elements, so building each one costs up to O(n). The extra factor of n accounts for constructing each result, not just reaching it.

drills.q: A candidate's subset-generation code appends path (the live list object) directly to the results list at every recursion node, instead of a copy. Walk through what the final results list looks like after the full traversal completes, and explain why.
drills.a: Since every entry in the results list is a reference to the SAME underlying path list object, and that object continues to be mutated (elements appended and popped) throughout the remainder of the traversal after each entry is 'recorded', every entry in the final results list will show whatever path looks like at the very end of the entire traversal -- typically empty, since backtracking pops every element back off by the time the whole recursion completes. The fix is to store a snapshot copy (e.g. path[:] in Python) at the moment each result is recorded, not the live reference.

drills.q: For Subsets II with input [1, 2, 2], sorted, walk through why skipping index i when nums[i] == nums[i-1] AND i > start correctly avoids duplicate subsets, and explain what would go wrong if you instead skipped whenever nums[i] == nums[i-1] regardless of the i > start condition.
drills.a: With i > start required: at the branching point where start=1 (after choosing the first '1'), the loop considers indices 1 and 2, both holding value 2; skipping index 2 (since nums[2]==nums[1] and 2 > start=1) prevents choosing the second '2' as an alternative sibling to the first '2' at this same branching point, avoiding a duplicate subset like [1,2] appearing twice. If instead you skipped ANY index where nums[i]==nums[i-1] with no start comparison, you would incorrectly skip legitimate uses of a repeated value across DIFFERENT recursion levels -- for example, you'd wrongly prevent including both 2's together in the same subset ([1,2,2]) at all, since the second 2 would always be skipped relative to the first regardless of whether they're actually siblings at the same branching point or sequential picks within one path.

drills.q: Derive the correct duplicate-skip condition for Permutations II and explain, with a concrete 3-element example, why simply checking nums[i]==nums[i-1] (without the used[i-1] check) produces wrong results.
drills.a: The correct condition: skip choosing nums[i] if nums[i]==nums[i-1] AND used[i-1] is False. Consider sorted input [1,1,2]. Without the used[i-1] check, as soon as the algorithm tries to place the second '1' (index 1) anywhere immediately after having just placed the first '1' (index 0) in the SAME active path (used[0]=True at that moment), the naive check nums[1]==nums[0] would still trigger and incorrectly skip using the second '1' even though it's legitimately needed to complete a valid permutation like [1,1,2] -- causing valid permutations to be silently dropped. The used[i-1]==False condition specifically restricts the skip to the case where the previous identical value was already tried AND fully backtracked out of (unused) at this same level in an earlier sibling branch -- that's the one specific situation duplication would otherwise occur, and only that situation.

drills.q: Combination Sum allows reusing the same array element multiple times; Combination Sum II does not. What is the single-line difference in the backtracking code between the two, and why does swapping it break each problem?
drills.a: Combination Sum recurses with start=i after choosing nums[i] (the same index remains eligible to be chosen again); Combination Sum II recurses with start=i+1 (only strictly-later, unused positions remain eligible). Using start=i+1 in Combination Sum would make it impossible to ever choose the same element twice, silently making valid combinations (that legitimately reuse a value) unreachable. Using start=i in Combination Sum II would allow the same array position to be chosen multiple times, producing invalid combinations that violate the 'each element used at most once' constraint.

drills.q: A candidate is asked to count how many subsets of a large array sum to exactly a target value, and reaches for backtracking with a running counter (no need to store or print the subsets). Is this a reasonable approach, and what's the better alternative?
drills.a: It's correct but exponential: the backtracking-with-counter approach still visits every one of the up to 2^n subset branches to check whether each one's sum matches the target, even though nothing is being printed or stored. The better alternative is a knapsack-style counting DP: dp[s] = number of ways to reach partial sum s using elements processed so far, updated for each new element by iterating s from target down to that element's value and adding dp[s - element] into dp[s]. This runs in O(n * target) time (pseudo-polynomial), because it reuses shared sub-computation across many different subsets that happen to reach the same intermediate sum, rather than tracking each subset individually.

drills.q: Explain how Permutation Sequence (finding the k-th permutation directly) avoids ever generating the first k-1 permutations, and state its complexity.
drills.a: It uses the factorial number system: at the first position, there are (n-1)! permutations for each choice of the first digit (since the remaining n-1 elements can be arranged in any order after it). Dividing the target index k by (n-1)! tells you exactly which remaining digit goes first; the remainder (k modulo (n-1)!) becomes the new target index for the second position, where there are now (n-2)! permutations per remaining choice, and so on. This process directly computes each digit of the answer using arithmetic on factorials and a shrinking pool of remaining digits, without ever constructing any permutation other than the target one. Complexity is O(n^2) (or O(n log n) with a Fenwick-tree-backed 'remove the k-th remaining element' structure), versus O(n!) to generate and index into the full list.
